summary: Proposes the Voice File Interchange Protocol (VFIP), a way to exchange speech files between different systems in the ARPA-Internet community. It is an early proposal that invites suggestions for improvement rather than a finished standard.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like agreeing on how to mail a tape recording so that any friend's tape player can play it, no matter what brand it is.

questions: how to exchange voice files between computers
what encoding methods does vfip support
subtitle: A format for exchanging voice and speech files between different systems over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Many systems can handle voice data, but each uses its own format, making it impossible to exchange recordings between systems from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: VFIP defines a standard 18-byte header that describes the voice data, including recording rate, duration, encoding method, and whether touch-tone signals are present.
tldr.outcome: Systems with registered VFIP headers can automatically convert speech files between formats and exchange them reliably.

today: RFC 978 is a proposed standard that was never widely adopted. Modern voice and multimedia systems use different formats like MP3, Ogg Vorbis, and OPUS instead of the VFIP structure.

sections.title: The Need for a Standard Voice Format
sections.content: As interest in voice and multimedia mail grew in the 1980s, many different systems started to support voice recordings. However, there was no standard way to exchange voice files between them. A recording made on one system could not be played on another system from a different vendor, making voice communication across the network impossible.
sections.plainLanguage: Different companies made different tape machines, and their tapes did not fit in other machines. This protocol lets anyone read any tape.

sections.title: The 18-Byte VFIP Header
sections.content: Every VFIP voice file starts with an 18-byte header. The header contains a version number (1 byte), the total header length in bytes (1 byte), a DTMF mask indicating which touch-tone digits are in the voice data (2 bytes), the recording rate in bits per second (4 bytes), the total duration in tenths of a second (4 bytes), and a 6-byte ASCII field for the encoding or recording method, padded with spaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is like a label on a cassette tape that tells you the recording speed, how long it is, and what kind of recorder made it.

sections.title: Encoding Methods
sections.content: The RFC lists several known encoding methods, including TI (Texas Instruments card for the IBM PC), IBM (PC Voice Communications Options), NVP-1 and NVP-2 (Network Voice Protocol), and COMPUT (Computalker card). The header's method field tells the receiving system which algorithm was used, so it can decode the voice data correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Different tape decks use different tricks to squeeze sound onto tape. The header tells you which trick was used.

references.text: Cohen, D., Specifications for the Network Voice Protocol (NVP), RFC 741, January 1976.
